units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Two things at once. A small, very old Belgian city that grew up on a muddy river.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the main home of the European Union.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And those two don't look much alike.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not at all. In one walk, you go from a medieval guild square to a glass office tower full of EU officials.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Let's do the mud first.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The river is called the Senne.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the name of the city comes from an old word meaning a home in the marsh.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Charming.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Honest, at least. People settled along that river, merchants on the road between Flanders and Cologne stopped here, and a market town grew.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How old are we talking?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The date people usually give is around the year nine seventy-nine.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A Frankish nobleman called Charles moved the relics of a saint named Gudula to a chapel on an island in the river.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels celebrated its thousandth birthday in 1979.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Is that exactly true?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Historians say the story is probably tidier than the reality.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the party was already booked.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The date stuck. Then came centuries of other people's empires.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Burgundy, Spain, Austria, France, the Netherlands.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Brussels has had a lot of landlords.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1830, a revolution. Belgium becomes its own country, with Brussels as the capital.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the second thing? The EU.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After the Second World War, Belgium was one of the six countries that founded what became the European Union.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels ended up with the European Commission and the Council, and the Parliament does much of its work here too.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which is why there are so many flags.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And so many languages. Which is the third thing.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Go on.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Brussels is officially bilingual, French and Dutch.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Every street sign has both. In daily life, most people speak French, but you'll hear Dutch, English, and dozens of other languages.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Nearly four in ten residents hold a foreign passport.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So don't be surprised if someone switches language mid-sentence.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Don't be surprised. And don't feel bad about starting in English.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I'll start in English and smile a lot.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A solid strategy.
